# Smart-Home Product Development Through 2035: From Connected Gadgets to Context-Aware Home Systems

The next phase of the smart-home industry will be shaped less by isolated connected gadgets than by coordinated systems that can sense household conditions, understand context, and act across multiple devices. The strongest product trends are AI-native multimodal assistants; interoperable, local-first hubs and gateways; home-energy systems combining solar, batteries, heat pumps, and bidirectional EV charging; passive health, aging-in-place, safety, and environmental monitoring; and increasingly capable cleaning and task-specific domestic robots. General-purpose companion and humanoid home robots are promising but remain less mature than robot vacuums, security devices, energy controllers, and passive sensors.

The evidence supports the direction of these trends more strongly than it supports an exact global ranking of future adoption. Market forecasts use different definitions, vendor announcements often report installed devices rather than active usage, and independent global data for AI assistants, general-purpose robots, residential HEMS, V2H/V2G, and aging-in-place deployments remain limited.

## Roadmap and evidence boundaries

This report first establishes the market baseline and explains why apparently conflicting market forecasts should not be combined. It then examines the transition from command-based devices to AI-native home control; the opportunities and practical limits of Matter and other interoperability approaches; the rise of home energy management and electrification products; the development of connected care, safety, and environmental intelligence; and the separation between mature cleaning robots and emerging general-purpose domestic robots.

The final sections consider privacy, cybersecurity, reliability, and accessibility as product features rather than secondary compliance issues. The conclusion identifies the specific product categories and feature sets most likely to define the industry's next phase, while distinguishing high-confidence product directions from promising but less proven ones.

## 1. Industry outlook and forces shaping future product development

### The smart home is becoming a system rather than a collection of devices

A smart home can be understood as a network of domestic appliances, sensors, connected devices, software, and services that provides monitoring, control, automation, support, and responsive services. The benefits span convenience, security, energy management, sustainability, health, and assisted living. The practical difference between a merely connected product and a genuinely smart product is the degree to which it can operate autonomously, communicate with other systems, and use contextual information from sensors.

A 2025 conceptual paper identifies those three elements as autonomy, connectivity, and context awareness. Autonomy means that a device can act without a direct user command; connectivity allows it to communicate with other devices or services; and context awareness allows it to interpret information from microphones, cameras, environmental sensors, or other inputs in relation to a situation rather than treating every command as isolated. [The AI and Society overview of smart devices](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-025-02182-4) places home automation, safety, health, and entertainment within this broader definition.

That distinction matters for product development. A connected light bulb controlled by an app is a useful smart-home component, but it does not by itself create an intelligent home. A more advanced system might infer that occupants are preparing for sleep, reduce lighting, adjust temperature, lock doors, and check whether appliances are operating. The future product opportunity lies in making those coordinated outcomes reliable, comprehensible, affordable, and controllable.

### Market estimates are large but measure different things

The global market is expanding, but there is no single harmonized market definition. Some estimates include devices, software, subscriptions, installation, and services; others count only physical consumer hardware. AI-specific forecasts isolate a smaller layer of the overall market, while HEMS and elder-care estimates cover adjacent categories with their own boundaries.

| Source and measure | Base estimate | Forecast | What it measures |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| [Mordor Intelligence](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/global-smart-homes-market-industry) | USD 140.42 billion in 2025 | USD 311.22 billion in 2031; 13.65% CAGR for 2026–2031 | Residential connected devices plus enabling software and services |
| [Technavio](https://www.technavio.com/report/smart-home-market-industry-analysis) | 2025 base year | USD 315.39 billion incremental growth from 2025 to 2030; 24.1% CAGR | Global market segmented by application, technology, channel, and geography |
| [Statista](https://www.statista.com/outlook/cmo/smart-home/worldwide/) | USD 159.5 billion in 2026 | USD 184.6 billion in 2031; 2.97% CAGR | Physical B2C smart-home-device revenue, excluding software, subscriptions, installation, and maintenance |
| [Next Move Strategy Consulting](https://www.nextmsc.com/report/ai-in-smart-home-market-ic5444) | USD 16.23 billion in 2025 | USD 148.75 billion in 2035; 24.8% CAGR | AI-specific smart-home devices, software, and services |
| [IEA-4E HEMS scan](https://www.iea-4e.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/DF6_HEMS-market-scan_Final.pdf) | Approximately USD 4 billion annually under a broad HEMS definition | Expected to treble by the end of the decade | Home-energy management systems and controllers |

These figures should be read as measures of different layers, not as values that can be added together. Statista's hardware-only estimate can be compared with physical-device sales, but not directly with Mordor's device-plus-services estimate. The AI forecast is a subset or adjacent layer within the broader smart-home economy, although the exact overlap is not disclosed. The IEA-4E figure covers home-energy management, which may also be counted within broader smart-home or energy-storage markets.

The strongest conclusion from the forecasts is therefore structural rather than numerical: the industry is moving from hardware-only value toward platform, software, orchestration, monitoring, and recurring-service value. That shift is visible in AI assistants, professional security monitoring, energy optimization, elder-care response services, and robot-as-a-service models.

### Adoption is growing, but the observed evidence is uneven

The 2025 ASHB survey found a reported smart-home technology adoption rate of 59% among 611 renters and homeowners in the United States and Canada, compared with 49% in its 2024 survey. Entertainment products led among adopters at 55%, followed by smart thermostats at 34%, security alarms and displays at 32%, smart lights and controllers at 31%, and access-control and recognition systems at 25%. [The ASHB 2025 survey](https://www.ashb.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Survey-Executive-Summary-3.pdf) is useful for identifying consumer priorities, but it is not a global adoption measurement.

NielsenIQ provides a different kind of evidence based on sales mix. In the first half of 2024, smart variants represented about 40% of global sales value for tumble dryers, washing machines, and dishwashers, with consumers paying approximately USD 300 more than for non-smart versions. Robot vacuums were substantially more mature: 95% of items sold were smart versions. The implication is that connectivity succeeds when it changes a clear use case, such as automatic cleaning, scheduling, remote monitoring, or energy control, rather than merely adding an app. [NielsenIQ's smart-home analysis](https://nielseniq.com/global/en/insights/analysis/2024/smart-home-2024-the-demand-and-price-dynamics-shaping-the-market/) also identifies cost as the leading overall barrier and privacy as the second-ranked barrier for smart appliances and security products, and the leading barrier for voice-assistant speakers.

The physical shape of the housing market also favors retrofit products. Mordor estimates that retrofit projects represented 64.36% of the smart-homes market in 2025 and projects a 14.12% CAGR through 2031. Its explanation is straightforward: in mature markets, the existing housing stock is roughly fifty times larger than new starts. Battery-powered sensors, solar-powered cameras, magnetic mounts, and wireless gateways can therefore expand the market more quickly than products dependent on new construction or extensive rewiring. [Mordor's retrofit analysis](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/global-smart-homes-market-industry) still notes that professional integrators remain important for high-end whole-home systems.

Multi-family housing is another underdeveloped channel. Single-family dwellings accounted for 71.63% of the 2025 market in Mordor's estimate, but the multi-family segment is forecast to grow at 17.46% through 2031. Landlords can deploy smart locks, thermostats, lighting, leak sensors, and centralized dashboards across many units, while portfolio purchasing can reduce per-unit costs. The constraints are split incentives, tenant privacy, condominium governance, and the need to provide unit-level personalization within a building-wide management system.

### Regional markets will develop along different paths

The global industry is not following one uniform adoption path. Mordor estimates that North America held 36.23% of smart-home revenue in 2025, while Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region at a projected 17.12% CAGR from 2026 to 2031. The AI-specific forecast from Next Move gives Asia-Pacific an even faster projected 28.1% CAGR through 2035, but this is a commercial forecast rather than an independent observed-adoption series.

| Region | Strongest product drivers | Main constraints |
|---|---|---|
| North America | Installed voice-assistant and security bases, professional monitoring, energy rebates, aging-in-place services, multi-family retrofit | Privacy concerns, high installation costs, fragmented subscriptions, uneven utility integration |
| Europe | Energy optimization, heat-pump and storage management, privacy-preserving AI, renovation and efficiency programs | Regulatory compliance, fragmented national energy systems, high expectations for data sovereignty |
| Asia-Pacific | Smart appliances, urban apartment systems, local electronics ecosystems, robotics, aging-in-place products | Diverse standards and income levels, regional fragmentation, uneven care and energy infrastructures |
| Latin America | Affordable Wi-Fi security, e-commerce distribution, mobile-first control, solar resilience products | Upfront cost, broadband and installation limitations, weaker after-sales support |
| Middle East and Africa | Premium residential automation, climate management, security, solar-powered and resilient devices | Uneven infrastructure, affordability, dependence on imported systems and professional installation |

The [Statista regional outlook](https://www.statista.com/outlook/cmo/smart-home/worldwide/) links Asia-Pacific demand to urbanization, rising middle-class incomes, robotic vacuums, smart entertainment, and smart kitchen appliances. Mordor similarly highlights lower-priced local ecosystems in parts of Asia-Pacific and the importance of broadband expansion. By contrast, European development is more closely tied to energy costs, privacy regulation, and building renovation, while North American development is supported by security, subscriptions, and an existing installed base.

These regional differences affect product design. A battery-powered, self-installed leak sensor with cellular fallback may be valuable in one market, while a professionally integrated heat-pump, battery, and dynamic-tariff system may be the more important product in another. A universal global product architecture remains possible, but the installation model, connectivity, energy controls, service model, and regulatory interface must often be localized.

### The historical transition: from automation to ambient and agentic systems

The industry's development can be understood as four overlapping transitions.

The first was the move from manual appliances to wired and programmable automation. Energy crises in the 1970s stimulated interest in household load management and home solar. Early systems used microcontrollers, personal computers, radio-frequency and ultrasonic sensors, powerline communication, and compact control interfaces. The [IEA-4E global HEMS scan](https://www.iea-4e.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/DF6_HEMS-market-scan_Final.pdf) describes this development as a long shift from early energy controllers toward connected thermostats, smart plugs, appliances, meters, solar, storage, and demand response.

The second was the consumer Internet-of-Things transition. Broadband, Wi-Fi, smartphones, cloud platforms, and lower-cost sensors made remote control practical. Smart thermostats, cameras, speakers, lighting, and plugs became independently marketable products. The value proposition was usually direct: control a device remotely, receive a notification, reduce energy use, or automate a routine.

The third was the ecosystem transition. As households accumulated products from multiple brands, separate apps and incompatible protocols became a major barrier. Proprietary platforms provided smoother experiences within one brand but increased lock-in. Gateways, hubs, cloud APIs, and multi-protocol controllers emerged to bridge the resulting fragmentation. The development of Matter from Project CHIP, backed by major ecosystem companies and led by the Connectivity Standards Alliance, represents the industry's attempt to create a common IP-based application layer.

The fourth transition is now under way: from connected control to context-aware and agentic systems. AI models can interpret natural language, combine voice, images, sensor data, and device states, and translate a high-level goal into several actions. In parallel, energy systems, care systems, and robots are moving from notification and scheduling toward prediction, optimization, and physical intervention.

The transition is not automatic. The evidence shows that convenience, security, energy savings, and care value can drive adoption, while cost, setup complexity, privacy, reliability, poor interoperability, and lack of trusted support can stop it. Future products will therefore succeed when intelligence is attached to a concrete, repeated household benefit and delivered through a system that remains understandable and controllable.

## 2. AI-native, context-aware, and personalized smart-home products

### The product is shifting from command execution to goal completion

Traditional voice assistants typically waited for a command such as “turn on the lights” or “set the thermostat.” AI-native assistants are being designed to interpret goals, use household context, and coordinate multiple services. A user might ask for a quiet evening, a cooler bedroom, or help arranging a repair; the system then determines which devices, services, or external providers are relevant.

This is the central product shift from command-response interaction to orchestration. The assistant becomes a software layer over devices, sensors, subscriptions, and third-party services. It can also become the main interface for the home, replacing the need to open separate applications.

The distinction between automation and AI is important. A fixed routine can turn lights on at a certain time. An AI-enabled system might modify that routine based on occupancy, weather, sleep patterns, energy prices, or a user's changing preference. That flexibility creates more value, but also increases the need for permission controls, explanations, verification, and safe failure modes.

### Current products illustrate several routes to AI-native control

The leading platforms are pursuing similar goals through different architectures and business models.

| Product or platform | Demonstrated direction | Evidence and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Google Gemini for Home | Conversational control, complex automations, AI descriptions for camera events, split-compute camera architecture | Google says Works with Google Home connects more than 800 million devices through cloud APIs and Matter; this is a platform-connected-device figure, not independent assistant usage |
| Amazon Alexa+ | Generative conversation, orchestration across services and devices, web-based task completion, subscription assistant | Amazon describes Alexa+ as built on Bedrock models, able to orchestrate tens of thousands of services and devices; it reports more than 600 million Alexa devices and a USD 19.99 monthly price outside Prime benefits |
| Samsung SmartThings AI Home | Personalized routines, control of Samsung and third-party devices, appliance screens as home interfaces | Samsung demonstrates routines that adjust air conditioning and lighting and a single tap that coordinates chores; the claims are company demonstrations |
| TELUS SmartHome Assistant | Generative user interfaces assembled from voice, images, sensor feeds, and video | TELUS says the system can unify more than 2,000 device models; the announcement describes an initial customer rollout rather than independent deployment evidence |
| Edge and hybrid assistants | Local wake-word detection, event recognition, privacy-preserving inference, cloud assistance for complex tasks | Research and standards work support the architecture, but hardware cost, model size, updates, and feature consistency remain constraints |

Google says its Gemini for Home program will add conversational control and complex automations to the Google Home platform. Its camera reference design uses on-device machine learning to send keyframes and metadata to the camera cloud, where event video and Gemini descriptions can be combined. This is a split-compute approach: the device performs an initial filtering task, while more computationally intensive interpretation occurs in the cloud. Google identifies Walmart's onn Indoor Camera Wired and onn Video Doorbell Wired as early partner products, with live view up to 1080p and intelligent alerts. [Google's Gemini for Home announcement](https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-for-home-expanding-the-platform-for-a-new-era-of-smart-home-ai/) presents these figures as platform and product information, not as an independent measure of usage.

Amazon's Alexa+ illustrates a more explicitly agentic model. Amazon says Alexa+ is built on large language models available through Amazon Bedrock and is designed to coordinate tens of thousands of services and devices, including web-based service arrangements such as booking repairs. The updated product article says more than 600 million Alexa devices are in use and lists a USD 19.99 monthly price, with free access for Prime members and regional variation in availability. [Amazon's Alexa+ description](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/new-alexa-generative-artificial-intelligence) is a vendor account, so the device count should not be treated as the number of active Alexa+ households.

Amazon also reports that Alexa+ customers engage two to three times more across a broader range of topics, increase smart-home engagement by nearly 50% in the first month, and set twice as many routines. Its developer toolkit for natural-language smart-home interactions was still described as being in Preview in the July 2026 update. These are useful signals about the intended business model and engagement direction, but they are company-reported metrics from Alexa+ customers rather than independent global adoption measures. [Amazon's developer update](https://developer.amazon.com/alexaplus/blogs/2026/07/alexa-plus-new-ways-to-build-experiences) provides the relevant qualification.

Samsung's AI Home strategy takes a more vertically integrated route. SmartThings connects Samsung and third-party devices, while Samsung's appliance portfolio supplies sensors, displays, and physical actuators. Its 2025 campaign shows SmartThings changing air-conditioning temperature and lighting through a routine and allowing a single tap to initiate coordinated appliance tasks. [Samsung's SmartThings AI Home campaign](https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-unveils-smartthings-meets-ai-home-campaign-ahead-of-ifa-2025) frames the home as an adaptive system rather than a set of independent appliances.

The appliance interface itself is also changing. Samsung has described refrigerators with 9-inch AI Home screens and ovens and laundry products with 7-inch displays. Its Map View feature turns an appliance screen into a control hub for connected devices. This approach treats the refrigerator, oven, washer, television, speaker, or display as a physical access point to the home system. It may be useful where household members prefer visual control, but it also risks multiplying screens and increasing product cost if the interface does not create a sufficiently valuable daily use case. [Samsung's appliance-screen announcement](https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-expands-ai-home-across-multiple-home-appliances-bringing-screens-everywhere-vision-to-life-ces-2025) describes the product direction but does not provide independent usage evidence.

TELUS takes the idea further with what it calls a Generative UI. Its SmartHome Assistant processes voice, images, sensor feeds, and videos in real time and dynamically creates a personalized interface. TELUS says the system can bring more than 2,000 device models into one interface. The important development is not simply another voice assistant; it is the use of AI to generate the form of interaction around the user's immediate need. [TELUS's 2026 launch announcement](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/telus-unveils-the-worlds-first-smart-home-ai-assistant-with-generative-ui-unifying-the-entire-connected-home-886174027.html) remains a company-reported product launch, and its rollout and long-term use were not independently measured in the supplied evidence.

### The AI architecture will usually be hybrid

The main architecture choice is not simply “AI” versus “no AI.” It is where inference happens, how much household data leaves the home, and which functions continue when the internet or cloud service is unavailable.

| Architecture | Strengths | Main limitations | Best-fit product uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cloud-centric AI | Large models, broad service integration, centralized updates, lower device-side hardware requirements | Latency, connectivity dependence, cloud data exposure, subscription dependence | Complex assistants, web tasks, large-scale analytics |
| Edge AI | Low latency, offline continuity, less raw data leaving the home, lower bandwidth use | Hardware cost, memory and power constraints, local update burden, smaller models | Wake-word detection, locks, cameras, alarms, local anomaly detection |
| Hybrid or split-compute AI | Combines local fast actions with cloud-scale reasoning and updates | More complex product architecture and data governance; unclear behavior when connectivity changes | Camera systems, whole-home assistants, energy optimization, care platforms |
| Multi-device distributed AI | Uses sensors, gateways, appliances, and cloud services together | Synchronization, permissions, versioning, interoperability, and debugging complexity | Context-aware home control, HEMS, passive care, robotics |

The 2025 edge-AI development article describes local processing as a way to reduce cloud dependence, latency, and exposure of sensitive voice or video data. It gives an illustrative smart-camera scenario in which local analysis could reduce energy use by 60%, reduce cloud data transformation by 12 terabytes per device annually, and bring response time within 200 milliseconds. Those values are presented as a possible example, not as a field trial. [The ACM edge-AI article](https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3745238.3745469) also describes Huawei's Full House Intelligence 4.0 as a system using distributed neural processing and edge-side intention understanding, but the reported accuracy and speed figures are product or system claims summarized by the article, not independent global benchmarks.

A hybrid design is often the practical compromise. A lock can recognize a known user locally and continue to operate during an internet outage, while a cloud service provides remote notification or longer-term analytics. A camera can detect motion and select keyframes locally, then use a cloud model to produce richer descriptions. A HEMS gateway can maintain safety rules and basic optimization locally while receiving tariffs, weather forecasts, or grid signals from the cloud.

The product requirement is therefore not simply “put AI on the device.” It is to define which decisions must remain local, which data may be shared, what happens when a model or connection fails, and how a user can see or override the result.

### Retrieval and modular orchestration make context usable

Large language models do not automatically know the current state of a home. They need access to device states, household preferences, calendars, tariffs, weather, maintenance information, and other current data. Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, combines retrieval from databases or specialized repositories with generation so that an assistant can use more current and relevant information. The 2025 [Future Internet paper on an AI smart-home orchestrator](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/17/5/198) identifies RAG as a way to improve context-aware responses in dynamic IoT settings, while noting the computational overhead of retrieving and managing multiple data sources.

A reliable assistant will therefore need more than a conversational model. It needs a device registry, a permission system, a state model, deterministic control interfaces, a safety policy, and an audit trail. Modular software architectures can help separate these functions. The same Future Internet paper discusses OSGi, in which service bundles can be deployed, updated, or removed independently, reducing disruptive system restarts. It also warns that modules must be synchronized to avoid dependency conflicts and security vulnerabilities.

This architecture explains why future smart-home platforms may become more valuable than individual devices. The platform can turn fragmented sensors and appliances into a coherent, personalized service. But the platform also becomes a point of concentration for privacy, security, service continuity, and vendor lock-in.

### Personalization will depend on trust and control

The consumer evidence suggests that AI adoption is conditional. In the ASHB survey, 32.4% of respondents reported current AI adoption. That figure rose in stated willingness when consumers were given more transparency and control: 53.8% were more likely to adopt with improved data transparency, and 53.2% were more interested when they could configure personalized AI workflows. Privacy concerns affected 43.5% specifically for AI applications, while setup complexity affected 27.9%.

These findings imply that personalization should not mean uncontrolled inference about household members. A product should allow users to select which routines are learned, which data are retained, which people can be recognized, and which actions require confirmation. It should distinguish between low-risk actions, such as changing lights, and high-risk actions, such as unlocking doors, turning off medical monitoring, changing a heat-pump safety limit, or initiating an emergency response.

The LLM reliability problem is especially serious in homes. The Future Internet paper cautions that language models can generate syntactically correct but semantically flawed code, misinterpret prompts, and overlook edge cases. In a household context, those errors can affect safety, privacy, energy costs, or physical property. [The paper's discussion of trustworthy smart-home orchestration](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-5903/17/5/198) points toward testing, formal verification, runtime monitoring, and human oversight.

### What the AI forecast can and cannot establish

The strongest supplied quantitative proxy for AI-native development is the Next Move Strategy Consulting forecast for the AI-in-smart-home market. It projects generative AI as the fastest-growing technology segment, from USD 0.49 billion in 2025 to USD 14.88 billion in 2035 at a 42.6% CAGR. It forecasts edge AI from USD 1.46 billion to USD 20.83 billion at 31.1%, and context awareness from USD 1.30 billion to USD 13.39 billion at 26.4%. Its offering categories project AI home robotics at a 27.6% CAGR and AI smart-home services at 37.9%.

Those figures measure forecast revenue segments, not observed assistant usage, unique households, or the number of homes with context-aware control. The supplied evidence does not include an independent, globally representative 2025–2026 usage series for AI assistants or a regional adoption forecast through 2030. Google and Amazon report very large installed-device bases, but those figures are not equivalent to active use of Gemini for Home or Alexa+.

The supported judgment is therefore conditional: AI-native assistants are likely to become a major product layer because leading platforms are redesigning their interfaces, device makers are adding sensors and compute, consumers show interest when control and transparency improve, and commercial forecasts place generative AI and edge AI among the fastest-growing segments. The speed and geographic distribution of adoption remain less certain than the direction of product development.

## 3. Interoperable ecosystems, hubs, and connected-device platforms

### Matter addresses the right problem, but not the whole problem

Smart-home interoperability has several layers. A device must communicate over a suitable physical or network technology, expose functions through a common application model, be discoverable and commissionable, and be supported by the controller or app that the consumer uses. Matter addresses the application and device-model layer over IP; it does not eliminate the need for Wi-Fi, Thread, Ethernet, border routers, controllers, bridges, or platform support.

The [Connectivity Standards Alliance](https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/) describes Matter as an IP-based standard for communication among smart-home devices, mobile apps, and cloud services. The standard can use Wi-Fi and Ethernet for higher-bandwidth products, Thread for low-power mesh devices, and Bluetooth Low Energy for commissioning. A Matter device still needs a controller, and Matter-over-Thread devices need a Thread Border Router.

The protocol alternatives remain complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

| Technology or approach | Best fit | Strength | Development constraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wi-Fi | Cameras, speakers, displays, appliances, high-bandwidth devices | Ubiquitous household infrastructure and high throughput | Higher power consumption and dependence on the home network |
| Zigbee or Z-Wave | Battery sensors, switches, locks, and low-power mesh products | Mature low-power operation and mesh networking | Often requires a dedicated hub or bridge; different application ecosystems |
| Thread | Battery sensors, locks, buttons, and other low-power Matter devices | IP-based low-power mesh without a non-IP translation layer | Requires border routers; network and multi-admin behavior can affect battery life |
| Matter | Cross-brand application interoperability | Common device models, secure commissioning, multi-platform potential | Certification does not guarantee feature parity, controller support, or reliable setup |
| Proprietary ecosystems | Vertically integrated product families | Deep features, controlled experience, fast coordination within one brand | Lock-in, limited product choice, difficult migration, and duplicated integrations |
| Multiprotocol gateways | Retrofit homes with mixed legacy devices | Bridges installed Zigbee, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi, Thread, and proprietary products | Hardware and software complexity, maintenance, and inconsistent feature mapping |

The 2024 [Electronics review of Matter and smart-home protocols](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics13112217) explains why different protocols will continue to coexist. A camera or speaker needs higher throughput than a door sensor; a battery sensor cannot use the same power budget as a plugged-in appliance. Matter can provide a shared application layer across those transport choices, but it does not make the underlying engineering trade-offs disappear.

### Matter's expanding device scope creates new product categories

Matter's early appeal was cross-brand control of lights, plugs, and basic sensors. Its scope is expanding toward the products that determine whether a home is genuinely coordinated. The CSA's Matter 1.4 description adds or expands support for energy devices such as solar panels, batteries, heat pumps, and water heaters, and enhances occupancy sensing with radar, vision, and ambient-sensing technologies. [The CSA's Matter 1.4 announcement](https://csa-iot.org/newsroom/matter-1-4-enables-more-capable-smart-homes/) also describes Home Routers and Access Points that combine Wi-Fi access points with Thread Border Routers and securely share Thread-network credentials.

Market analysis of the 2026 specification landscape identifies major appliances, cameras and doorbells, robot vacuums, soil sensors, and energy-management devices as important additions. [Consumer Tech Wire's 2026 Matter analysis](https://consumertechwire.com/analysis/matter-1-4-and-the-state-of-smart-home-interop-2026/) emphasizes that specification coverage and actual user experience are separate questions.

The scale of the Matter ecosystem is also reported inconsistently. The CSA describes Matter products as being in millions of homes and supported by hundreds of member companies and thousands of engineers. Mordor reports more than 500 certified products from 200 manufacturers by late 2025, while another 2026 summary reports more than 4,000 certified devices. These counts cannot be reconciled from the supplied evidence because they may use different dates, certification definitions, and counting methods. They demonstrate growing industry participation, not a reliable global adoption total.

### Open standards and proprietary features solve different problems

An open standard reduces the risk that a consumer will buy a device that cannot join an existing home. It also lets manufacturers use one baseline implementation across multiple ecosystems. This is valuable for retrofit products, online retail, and households that combine brands.

A proprietary ecosystem can still provide deeper product value. Premium lighting systems may offer effects, synchronization, or sensor behaviors that Matter does not expose. An appliance brand may coordinate its compressor, motor, display, and maintenance data more deeply within its own platform than it can through a common standard. The practical future is therefore likely to be a two-layer model: Matter for baseline discovery, control, and portability; proprietary extensions for differentiated features.

| Alternative | Cross-brand compatibility | Feature depth | Local-control potential | Main consumer risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Proprietary platform | Strong within one brand or partner network | Often highest within that network | Depends on vendor | Lock-in and migration cost |
| Matter baseline | Broad in principle across participating platforms | Limited to supported device types and clusters; vendor extensions may remain separate | Designed for local LAN operation, with cloud used for remote access or services | A Matter logo may not reveal which functions each platform supports |
| Local multiprotocol platform | Broad across Matter and legacy protocols | Can expose advanced integrations through community or vendor work | Often strong when self-hosted or locally controlled | Setup, maintenance, and technical skill requirements |
| Bespoke cloud gateway | Potentially broad through custom APIs | Can optimize selected devices deeply | Often cloud-dependent | Integration breaks, subscription dependence, and opaque compatibility |

The IEA-4E HEMS scan shows why this distinction matters. In its 51-product review, about one-fifth of HEMS products operated in a closed ecosystem, a similar proportion used open standards, and 53% relied on bespoke integrations for each brand or model. Bespoke integration is a practical response to incomplete standards, but it duplicates engineering work and makes product support expensive. The [IEA-4E market scan](https://www.iea-4e.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/DF6_HEMS-market-scan_Final.pdf) concludes that open standards need clear protocol requirements and compliance testing, not merely a claim of compatibility.

### Certification does not guarantee a consistent user experience

The supplied 2026 evidence shows why interoperability remains an implementation risk. Consumer Tech Wire compared Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Samsung SmartThings and found that each implemented a different subset of the Matter specification. It described Apple as lacking support for some Matter 1.4 major-appliance types in the cited release, Google as broad but less reliable, Amazon as more predictable but ecosystem-locked, and SmartThings as comparatively complete and consistent. These are editorial testing conclusions, not a standardized industry benchmark.

The same analysis reports quarterly installation testing across approximately 60 device combinations, with Thread mesh problems the largest category of installation failure in its 2026 sample. A separate 2026 review describes examples in which a Matter device's supported functions differed between Google Home and Amazon Alexa, and in which an IKEA leak detector could not integrate with Alexa because leak sensors were not yet supported there. [The Matter Smart Home status review](https://matter-smarthome.de/en/development/the-matter-standard-in-2026-a-status-review/) stresses that both device certification and platform certification determine what a user can actually do.

Amazon's own developer documentation illustrates the same boundary. Alexa-compatible Matter products must use a current Matter SDK, belong to an Alexa-supported device category, and implement required clusters. Echo and eero devices may act as Thread Border Routers, but Amazon supports only a subset of Matter 1.5 and earlier device types. [Amazon's Matter developer guidance](https://developer.amazon.com/docs/alexaplus/smarthome/matter-support.html) is therefore a product-support matrix, not a guarantee that every Matter function will appear in Alexa.

There is no standardized independent cross-platform test in the supplied evidence covering Matter 1.4 and 1.5 across Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Home Assistant, including advanced feature support, setup reliability, and battery effects. The strongest available evidence is a mixture of platform documentation, editorial testing, troubleshooting reports, and individual product observations. That is sufficient to identify implementation risk, but not to calculate a universal failure rate.

### Battery life is an interoperability metric

Low-power products reveal a less visible problem. A battery sensor that joins multiple Matter fabrics may need to communicate with more controllers, maintain additional state, or respond to more discovery and polling traffic. XDA Developers reports one example in which a battery sensor's claimed three-year life fell to 18 months when it communicated with Apple Home, Google Home, and Home Assistant. [The XDA analysis](https://www.xda-developers.com/why-matter-isnt-the-smart-home-savior-we-were-promised-yet/) presents this as a multi-admin chatter problem, not as a standardized measurement.

A 2026 Matter status review gives a different product-level comparison: Aqara's FP300 multi-sensor is specified for up to three years on Zigbee and more likely two years on Thread, with unstable Thread networks, weak border-router connections, and Multi-Admin polling potentially shortening real-world life. Another guide says Matter allows up to five fabrics, but many first-generation devices are stable with only two or three. [The FixyNest Multi-Admin guide](https://fixynest.com/matter-multi-admin-second-controller-kicks-first/) makes the important distinction between advertised fabric slots and stable operation.

This creates a direct product-development trade-off:

- More ecosystems can mean more consumer choice and greater product reach.
- More fabrics can increase memory, communication, and test requirements.
- Thread can reduce power relative to Wi-Fi, but a poorly managed mesh or multi-admin configuration can erase part of that advantage.
- A product may need to prioritize one fabric for low-power operation while exposing other platforms through a gateway or synchronized state model.

Future Matter products will therefore need better battery-aware scheduling, fabric management, border-router diagnostics, and user-visible compatibility information. “Works with Matter” is becoming a starting point rather than a sufficient product specification.

### The next infrastructure products will be hubs, routers, bridges, and diagnostic layers

The likely growth of interoperable smart homes does not mean hubs disappear. It changes what they do. A hub may combine a Thread Border Router, Wi-Fi access point, Matter controller, Zigbee or Z-Wave bridge, local automation engine, security boundary, and backup power supply.

The 2020 [Sensors gateway study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7285766/) shows the historical problem: commercial gateways supported different device counts, from 70 to more than 300 in the products it compared, and no gateway covered every available device. Its proposed dynamically updatable gateway downloaded device profiles and exposed APIs without requiring a full gateway software update. That idea remains relevant even in a Matter environment because new device types, optional features, and vendor extensions will continue to evolve.

The product opportunity is not only a consumer hub. It includes:

- routers that prioritize and diagnose smart-home traffic;
- Matter and Thread commissioning assistants;
- multiprotocol bridges for legacy devices;
- local controllers that continue during cloud outages;
- capability directories that explain which features a platform actually supports;
- fleet-management tools for landlords and care providers;
- battery and mesh-health diagnostics;
- secure, remotely updateable gateways.

Interoperability will become a differentiator when it reduces the work required to install, maintain, replace, and expand a home. It will not be complete merely because devices share a common logo.

## 4. Energy management, electrification, and sustainability products

### HEMS turns the home into an energy asset

A Home Energy Management System connects multiple residential energy devices and a communications network to monitor and control household generation, storage, and consumption. It may coordinate solar PV, batteries, EV chargers, water heating, HVAC, pool pumps, smart appliances, lighting, and plug loads. Basic systems show consumption and allow scheduling; more advanced systems optimize solar self-consumption, energy cost, backup readiness, or participation in external markets.

The [IEA-4E HEMS definition and market scan](https://www.iea-4e.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/DF6_HEMS-market-scan_Final.pdf) distinguishes four levels:

1. Monitoring without meaningful control.
2. Basic scheduling of multiple devices.
3. Sophisticated in-home optimization based on live system data and user objectives.
4. Orchestrated control that responds to external market or network signals.

The 51-product scan is important because it separates advertised potential from current functionality. Under a cautious interpretation, 34% of products offered monitoring, 30% basic control, 24% sophisticated optimization, and 12% orchestrated control. Under the highest stated claims, only 6% were monitoring-only, 10% basic, 51% sophisticated, and 33% orchestrated. The gap shows how quickly vendors are announcing capabilities and how difficult it is for customers to determine what is actually available across their particular equipment.

### HEMS architectures expose a retrofit trade-off

The main product architectures have different installation, reliability, and integration characteristics.

| HEMS architecture | Installation and cost | Strengths | Weaknesses | Likely role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Separate local gateway | Often requires dedicated hardware; 39% of scanned products were simple to install, while 57% required an electrician in some form | Fast local control, backup operation, household-level coordination | Upfront hardware and installation cost; many bespoke integrations | Retrofit homes and mixed-device households |
| Integrated inverter, battery, or meter control | Installed with another energy asset | Lower marginal installation cost and deep control of the host system | Can create brand lock-in and incomplete whole-home coverage | Solar-plus-storage and electrification packages |
| Cloud platform without local hardware | Low physical installation cost; relies on APIs and compatible devices | Easy scaling, analytics, virtual power-plant participation | Internet dependence, latency, cloud privacy, API changes | Retailer, utility, and subscription-based programs |
| Hybrid gateway and cloud | Local rules and controls plus cloud analytics, tariffs, and grid signals | Balances response time, resilience, and advanced optimization | More complex architecture and commissioning | Likely mainstream architecture for sophisticated HEMS |

In the IEA-4E scan, 61% of products were separate devices, 21% required no additional hardware because control occurred through compatible cloud systems, and 18% were integrated into existing equipment. Hybrid control was the dominant cloud architecture at 69%, compared with 23% that were predominantly cloud-based. The report notes that local functions can continue during internet disruption, while cloud functions support forecasting, dynamic tariffs, demand response, and virtual power plants.

The consumer proposition also depends on the scale of coordination. A programmable thermostat can save energy, but a system that coordinates HVAC, water heating, solar, storage, and EV charging can shift loads across the day and provide backup. The IEA-4E report cites estimates ranging from 3% savings for programmable thermostats to 26% for integrated monitoring and control, while warning that household behavior and system configuration produce wide variation.

### Energy cost, resilience, and decarbonization are converging

The strongest drivers of energy-management product development are no longer only environmental. They include electricity prices, peak-demand charges, outages, solar self-consumption, battery payback, grid constraints, and energy independence.

In the ASHB survey, 35.0% of respondents identified high energy costs as their primary home challenge. Meanwhile, 28.6% wanted real-time energy monitoring and 24.6% wanted automated optimization. Utilities had the highest data-sharing comfort score among the entities measured, at 3.74 out of 5.0. This suggests that utilities, retailers, and energy-service companies may be trusted routes for selling or financing integrated energy products, although the survey is limited to the United States and Canada.

Mordor links connected thermostats to occupancy learning and demand-response signals and reports possible savings of 10%–23%. Those savings are an analyst estimate rather than a universal field result, and actual performance depends on building quality, climate, tariffs, HVAC systems, and user preferences. The product-development implication is nevertheless clear: occupancy sensors, weather forecasts, tariff data, and demand-response controls are becoming part of the same product value proposition.

The HEMS market is also moving from individual devices toward all-in-one energy systems. IMARC identifies integrated residential storage units that combine a battery, hybrid inverter, and energy-management system in one enclosure as a way to reduce installation complexity and labor. It estimates the global residential energy-storage-system market at USD 1.46 billion in 2025 and USD 6.31 billion by 2034, but that estimate is a commercial market forecast with its own scope. [IMARC's residential storage analysis](https://www.giiresearch.com/report/imarc2032924-residential-energy-storage-system-market-size.html) reports Europe as the largest regional share in 2025 and Asia-Pacific as the fastest-growing region.

### Batteries are becoming software-managed household infrastructure

The physical battery is only one component of the future product. The more consequential product combines storage hardware with forecasting, tariff optimization, backup control, safety monitoring, and grid participation.

The IEA projects that a significant share of battery storage added through 2030 will be behind the meter and paired with rooftop solar, including batteries aggregated into virtual power plants. In its scenarios, the behind-the-meter battery-pack market grows from USD 4 billion in 2023 to USD 7 billion in 2030 under the Stated Policies Scenario and USD 8 billion under the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario. [The IEA battery outlook](https://www.iea.org/reports/batteries-and-secure-energy-transitions/executive-summary) describes those figures as scenario projections, not observed household deployment.

BNEF's 2025 survey, as reported by Solar Analytica, puts the global average lithium-ion pack price at USD 108 per kWh in 2025 and behind-the-meter stationary-storage pack prices at USD 70 per kWh, down 45% year on year. The same source reports 112 GW and 307 GWh of new global storage additions in 2025 and forecasts 158 GW and 459 GWh in 2026. Utility-scale storage represented about 85% of 2025 additions, so the global totals should not be interpreted as residential installations. [The Solar Analytica summary of BNEF and residential-storage data](https://solaranalytica.com/global-behind-the-meter-storage-2025) also cites a forecast that customer-sited residential and commercial storage could reach approximately 25% of global installations by 2030.

The likely residential products are therefore:

- modular, stackable LFP battery systems;
- all-in-one battery, inverter, and HEMS units;
- plug-in or balcony storage for lower-friction retrofits;
- solar diverters and heat-pump water-heater controls;
- outage-aware home energy gateways;
- VPP interfaces that let utilities or aggregators coordinate household batteries;
- software that optimizes among bill savings, comfort, battery life, emissions, and backup readiness.

The 2026–2027 [MateSolar residential solar-plus-storage outlook](https://www.mate-solar.com/global-residential-solar-energy-storage-blue-paper-2026-2027/) identifies modular systems and LFP chemistry as major product directions and forecasts predictive and prescriptive HEMS using consumption, weather, and grid data. Its LFP cycle-life figure of more than 6,000 cycles to 80% depth of discharge is a technology forecast rather than a universal product guarantee. The IEA also warns that battery growth will increase demand for lithium, nickel, graphite, manganese, and cobalt, while chemistry innovation, recycling, and right-sizing could reduce critical-mineral demand. Sustainable product development must therefore consider not only operational energy savings but also materials, replacement, recycling, and battery longevity.

Zendure's September 2026 announcement illustrates the direction toward “agentic HEMS.” It describes a system in which one model forecasts solar generation, weather, prices, and household loads; another agent layer chooses among cost, comfort, safety, and battery-life objectives; and an operating system coordinates solar, batteries, heat pumps, EVs, tariffs, and common household loads. Zendure's compatibility and provider-coverage numbers are vendor claims, not independent performance evidence, but the architecture reflects a broader shift from dashboards to autonomous energy planning. [Zendure's Agentic HEMS announcement](https://www.prnewswire.com/il/news-releases/zendure-introduces-agentic-hems-at-ifa-2026-the-home-energy-hub-of-the-ai-era-302867966.html) also describes modular SolarFlow storage, a central PowerHub, plug-and-play retrofit storage, and a smart wallbox.

### EVs extend the home-energy system beyond the house

Electric vehicles create a large, mobile battery resource. Smart charging can move charging to low-price or high-renewable periods; V2H can supply the home during an outage or reduce grid imports; V2G can allow an aggregator or utility to use the vehicle for grid services.

The EV base is expanding. BloombergNEF forecasts 23.3 million passenger EV sales globally in 2026, an 11% increase from 2025, with growth across China, Europe, Southeast Asia, India, Mexico, and Brazil. The IEA's scenarios project electric-car sales reaching 41 million in 2030 under STEPS or 59 million under the Net Zero Scenario, while average EV battery prices in the Net Zero Scenario fall from USD 139 per kWh in 2023 to USD 80 per kWh in 2030. These are scenarios, not guaranteed outcomes. [The BloombergNEF 2026 EV outlook](https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/electric-vehicle-outlook/) and [the IEA battery report](https://www.iea.org/reports/batteries-and-secure-energy-transitions/executive-summary) provide the relevant forecasts.

Bidirectional charging products are already being announced. Enphase's IQ Bidirectional EV Charger architecture targets 400- and 800-volt vehicles and up to 11.5 kW of bidirectional power, with optimization based on electricity prices, solar forecasts, and grid conditions. Enphase expected availability in the second half of 2026 and described standards compliance as an expectation, not a demonstrated result. [Enphase's announcement](https://investor.enphase.com/news-releases/news-release-details/enphase-energy-unveils-new-iq-bidirectional-ev-charger) therefore illustrates a product direction rather than independent deployment data.

The implementation barriers are substantial. V2G requires compatible vehicles, bidirectional chargers, communication protocols, utility programs, interconnection rules, battery-warranty arrangements, and regulatory permission. The [Mobility House analysis of V2G implementation](https://mobilityhouse-energy.com/int_en/knowledge-center/article/implementing-v2g) describes the need for coordinated hardware, standardized communication, and legal frameworks. It also cites an Agora Energiewende scenario in which 25% of EVs use V2G by 2035 and 40% of those vehicles are available to the electricity market, producing 28 GW of short-duration usable capacity. That is a conditional scenario, not a deployment forecast.

Regulatory standards are moving in the same direction. The Mobility House source reports that ISO 15118-20 becomes mandatory for certain newly installed or modernized publicly accessible charging points in the European context from January 1, 2027, supporting smart charging and V2G functions. The requirement does not establish that residential V2H/V2G adoption will be widespread, but it provides a standards target for product development.

### Regional energy archetypes will differ

The [MateSolar global residential-storage analysis](https://www.mate-solar.com/global-residential-solar-energy-storage-blue-paper-2026-2027/) distinguishes three regional archetypes:

- Post-subsidy optimization in Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Japan, and Australia, where the focus is on maximizing solar self-consumption and reducing bills.
- Resilience and grid services in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and France, where outages, tariffs, and grid participation add value.
- Fundamental electrification and security in parts of Latin America, the Caribbean, and South Africa, where reliability, access, and backup may matter more than sophisticated market participation.

The IEA-4E scan makes a related distinction: North American and European products show more emphasis on controlling household loads, while Australia has more products focused on solar generation and storage. These differences mean a global HEMS platform must support multiple objectives rather than assuming that every household values the same optimization target.

The strongest energy product trend is thus not a standalone smart thermostat or battery. It is a coordinated, expandable household energy system that can begin with monitoring or a single controller and grow into solar, storage, heat pumps, EV charging, backup, and external grid services. Low-friction installation and honest savings estimates will be as important as optimization algorithms.

### The independent evidence gap

The supplied evidence does not provide a single independent global dataset for residential HEMS, V2H, V2G, and behind-the-meter storage deployments by region through 2030. The IEA-4E scan measures products available in the market, not installed market share; BNEF scenarios measure energy-storage growth across utility and customer-sited segments; Australian data provide a strong country example, with SunWiz reporting 221,000 residential systems installed in 2025 and battery ownership reaching 4.6% of homes; and commercial forecasts provide broader market proxies.

These sources support the conclusion that energy-management products are a major development direction. They do not support a precise global ranking of HEMS, V2H, V2G, or residential-storage adoption by 2030.

## 5. Health, aging-in-place, environmental monitoring, and safety products

### Aging creates structural demand for connected care

The aging population and shortage of caregivers create a long-term demand base for smart-home health and care products. Fritz and colleagues cite an estimated global population of 1.6 billion adults aged 65 and older by 2050. They also cite a projected decline in the U.S. caregiver-to-older-adult ratio for people aged 80 and older from 7:1 in 2010 to 3:1 by 2050. [The 2026 study by Fritz and colleagues](https://aging.jmir.org/2026/1/e88290/PDF) frames smart-home monitoring as one way to extend support while preserving independence.

A commercial estimate from DataIntelo values the global smart-home elder-care market at USD 14.8 billion in 2025 and projects USD 42.6 billion by 2034 at a 12.5% CAGR. It estimates North America at 38.4% of 2025 revenue, Europe at 27.6%, and Asia-Pacific at 23.1%, with Asia-Pacific forecast to grow fastest at 15.2% through 2034. Monitoring devices represented 34.2% of the 2025 product mix, safety and security 27.8%, health-management devices 19.4%, and smart-home appliances 12.6%. [DataIntelo's elder-care market report](https://dataintelo.com/report/smart-home-elder-care-market) is a commercial estimate spanning monitoring, safety, appliances, and connected health; it should not be treated as a measured deployment census.

The product development consequence is a shift from isolated medical-alert devices toward connected care ecosystems. A future care package may combine passive motion and contact sensors, radar, environmental data, wearable or room-based vital-sign sensing, medication support, voice interaction, a caregiver dashboard, and a defined human response workflow.

### The core technical choice is how to sense without intruding

Smart-home health monitoring can use wearable, ambient, visual, radar, acoustic, pressure, or multimodal sensors. Each alternative trades privacy, coverage, accuracy, installation, battery life, and user burden.

| Sensing approach | Product examples | Strengths | Main limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wearables | Accelerometers, gyroscopes, GPS, pulse and vital-sign devices | Direct body data, mobility tracking, emergency communication | Must be worn, charged, maintained, and accepted; discomfort and forgetfulness |
| Ambient sensors | PIR, door and cabinet contacts, bed and chair sensors, smart carpets | Passive, low burden, relatively privacy-preserving | Indirect inference; routines vary; limited physiological detail |
| Radar and radio sensing | mmWave, Wi-Fi sensing, Doppler, non-contact motion sensors | Can work without cameras or wearables; useful for room-level activity and falls | Installation, calibration, multipath, and validation challenges |
| Cameras and thermal imaging | RGB, depth, infrared, thermal cameras | Rich spatial and posture information | Surveillance concerns, lighting and occlusion, greater data sensitivity |
| Multimodal systems | Motion plus radar, pressure, audio, environmental and wearable data | Redundancy, contextual interpretation, better differentiation of events | Cost, synchronization, privacy governance, model complexity |

The 2022 scoping review by Kim and colleagues identified six major functions: daily activities, abnormal behavior, cognitive impairment, falls, indoor positioning, and sleep quality. Of 30 studies, 27 focused on functional monitoring and only three on social interaction. Passive infrared motion sensors appeared in 21 studies and contact sensors in 19. [Kim and colleagues' review](https://www.i-jmr.org/2022/2/e39005/) shows why low-burden environmental sensing remains central to aging-in-place products.

The review also describes privacy-oriented alternatives to cameras. One 128-sensor smart carpet measured gait parameters and fall risk. A millimeter-wave radar and convolutional-neural-network system reported 98.74% accuracy with an average prediction time of 51.4 milliseconds in its study, while a Wi-Fi-based system reported 95% detection in both line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight conditions. These are prototype or study results, not guarantees of commercial performance in uncontrolled homes.

Wearables remain valuable where direct vital or motion data are necessary, but long-term adherence is difficult. A systematic review of 31 aging-in-place studies found only six using wearables and identified short battery life, maintenance, discomfort, and skin reactions as constraints. Environmental sensing is therefore likely to grow alongside, rather than be replaced by, wearable products.

### Fall detection is moving from alarms toward multimodal care workflows

Fall detection is one of the clearest examples of the shift from reactive notification to contextual intervention. Earlier products required a person to press a panic button or wear a device. Newer systems seek to detect a fall automatically, distinguish it from sitting or bending, estimate severity, identify repeated near-falls, and route alerts to family members, caregivers, clinicians, or emergency services.

A 2025 [scoping review of 73 fall-detection studies across 33 countries](https://www.jamda.com/article/S1525-8610(24)00752-7/fulltext) identifies four technology groups: motion and body sensors, imaging and visual systems, environmental sensors, and robotic or autonomous systems. Machine-learning methods appear in 35 studies, support-vector machines in 17, and convolutional neural networks in 11. Reported accuracy ranges from 75% to 100%, but 29 studies did not specify performance criteria. More importantly, 83% of the studies were preclinical trials focused on technical evaluation, usability, or feasibility.

This evidence supports the technical direction but limits the strength of commercial claims. Simulated falls in controlled rooms are easier to classify than real falls involving different body types, mobility aids, clothing, lighting, pets, furniture, and overlapping household activity. A product that reports high laboratory accuracy may still produce too many false alarms or miss atypical real-world events.

The most promising product architecture is therefore multimodal and human-centered:

- passive room sensing to reduce the burden of wearables;
- radar, pressure, contact, or acoustic signals to complement motion data;
- optional wearable or vital-sign information;
- local or edge inference for low latency and reduced raw-video exposure;
- personalized thresholds based on the individual's mobility and routine;
- confidence levels and explanations rather than an unexplained binary alarm;
- escalation rules that distinguish a low-confidence anomaly from a likely emergency;
- two-way communication and a human response pathway.

A 2026 prototype study by Fritz and colleagues provides a useful example of both promise and limitation. The system used six multisensors per home and generated alerts for social isolation, reduced activity, kitchen use, hygiene, restless nights, and changing sleep routines. It monitored 48 older adults in 48 homes in the U.S. Pacific Northwest, generated 37 million sensor readings, 1.2 million high-level events, and 4,719 novel alerts, and produced 72 clinical interventions. The system was not intended to detect or manage emergencies.

Only 1.57% of initial email alerts received a participant response, compared with 7.79% of follow-up SMS alerts. Community health workers and registered nurses responded to approximately 78.3% of escalated alerts, although the paper contains slightly different figures in two passages. No action was required for 93% of alerts. Participants rated the system highly among respondents, with a mean likelihood-to-recommend score of 8.68 out of 10 from 33 respondents, but many preferred phone calls to automated alerts and 15 of 63 consenters withdrew for reasons including privacy, perceived invasiveness, and time constraints. [Fritz and colleagues' prospective mixed-methods study](https://aging.jmir.org/2026/1/e88290/PDF) demonstrates that a technically functioning alert system still depends on communication preferences, cultural expectations, caregiver capacity, and human follow-up.

The product lesson is that “fall detection” should not be treated as a sensor feature alone. The value lies in a complete chain from sensing to interpretation, alert prioritization, human response, documentation, and prevention. The [2026 fall-detection assessment by 360iResearch](https://www.360iresearch.com/library/intelligence/fall-detection-system) describes the market's movement from standalone panic buttons toward systems combining motion, location, environmental monitoring, and two-way communication, while emphasizing representative training data, transparent performance testing, bias safeguards, and human review.

### Medication support and vital-sign monitoring are promising but less independently verified

Medication-management systems can include connected dispensers, dose verification, reminders, caregiver notifications, and escalation when a dose is missed. Vital-sign products can monitor blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, glucose, or other measures and share them with care teams.

Commercial market estimates identify health-management devices as a fast-growing category. DataIntelo projects a 13.8% CAGR for the segment through 2034. Another commercial estimate for technology-enabled in-home senior-care monitoring places fall-detection wearables at 42.5% of 2025 revenue, vital-sign sensors at 33.8%, and medication-management systems at 23.7%, with vital-sign sensors forecast to grow fastest. [The Research Intelo monitoring-device report](https://researchintelo.com/report/technology-enabled-in-home-senior-care-monitoring-devices-market) describes these figures as market estimates and cites pilot outcomes, including improved fall-risk scoring and reported reductions in fall incidence.

The supplied evidence does not establish global deployment scale for medication-management systems or caregiver-response products. Nor does it provide a globally comparable rate of clinical validation. The strongest supported conclusion is that these products are likely to grow where reimbursement, health-system integration, and caregiver workflows exist, but their medical and commercial value depends on validated measurements and a response organization. A device that generates an alert without anyone responsible for acting on it has limited practical value.

### Environmental intelligence is becoming a safety and wellness product family

Indoor environmental monitoring is moving beyond a single smoke or carbon-monoxide alarm. Consumers increasingly want continuous information about air quality, humidity, water use, leaks, temperature, and ventilation, especially when those measurements can produce understandable guidance or trigger mitigation.

The ASHB survey found that air and water quality was a priority for 38.8% of respondents, while environmental comfort was a priority for 36.6%. It also found demand for real-time water monitoring at 21% and strong interest in real-time energy monitoring. These results are limited to the United States and Canada, but they align with a broader product shift from event-only alarms to continuous environmental intelligence.

Ruuvi Air, launched in September 2025, illustrates the air-quality direction. It measures temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, volatile organic compounds, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, and air pressure. Ruuvi combines those readings into a proprietary indoor-air-quality score from 0 to 100 and presents daily guidance through an app. [Ruuvi's product announcement](https://ruuvi.com/introducing-ruuvi-air-smart-indoor-air-quality-sensor/) describes the product as a move from reactive alerts toward continuous wellness management. Its distribution to customers in more than 150 countries is a company-reported distribution figure, not evidence of Ruuvi Air adoption.

Water management illustrates the move from detection to intervention. Shelly Flood Gen4 supports Wi-Fi, Zigbee, and Bluetooth, uses a cable that can detect water along its length, and allows multiple cables to extend coverage up to 150 meters. It can be linked to devices that automatically shut off washing machines or dishwashers. The sensor checks flood-state changes every five seconds to balance battery life and response time. [Shelly's Flood Gen4 product information](https://us.shelly.com/products/shelly-flood-gen4) makes the trade-off explicit: a battery product must balance immediate detection with power consumption.

Flume's water monitor tracks indoor and outdoor use continuously, sends leak alerts, and can notify a friend or neighbor. That is a different response model from a siren: it distributes awareness to a person who may be able to intervene. [Flume's product information](https://flumewater.com/) illustrates the extension from sensor to remote response.

The broader trend is a closed-loop safety product:

1. Sense an environmental condition continuously.
2. Interpret whether it is normal, unusual, or dangerous.
3. Explain the condition in plain language.
4. Recommend an action or take a bounded automatic action.
5. Notify the right household member, caregiver, utility, or service provider.
6. Record what happened without retaining unnecessary raw data.

This pattern applies to leaks, air quality, smoke, temperature extremes, appliance faults, and potentially energy or care events.

### Aging-in-place products need accessibility by design

Aging-in-place technology will not scale if it assumes that every user is comfortable with smartphones, small text, touchscreens, subscriptions, and complex configuration. The [ISO/TS 25558:2026 specification](https://www.iso.org/standard/85086.html) provides a process for assessing the needs of older people and selecting, applying, and evaluating smart-home products as health conditions and lifestyles change.

Human-centered features include large physical controls, voice operation, adjustable text and contrast, clear audio and visual alerts, multilingual or culturally adaptable interaction, low-maintenance sensors, caregiver permissions, and the ability to contact a person rather than only a bot. Fakhimi's discussion of smart-home support for older adults also identifies tracking sleep, social withdrawal, and speech changes as possible ways to generate early prompts, while emphasizing usability, accessibility, encryption, transparent policies, and user-controlled permissions. [Fakhimi's 2025 essay](https://doi.org/10.5888/pcd22.250113) presents these as prospective directions rather than validated clinical outcomes.

The best aging-in-place products will therefore be multi-generational rather than visibly medical. A leak sensor, voice assistant, smart lock, thermostat, and lighting system can serve the entire household while also supporting an older resident. This reduces stigma and makes the product more likely to remain installed when care needs change.

## 6. Domestic robotics and multimodal home-assistance products

### Robot vacuums are mature; general-purpose home robots are not

Domestic robotics needs to be separated into at least three categories:

- mature cleaning robots, especially robot vacuums and floor cleaners;
- task-specific appliance or service robots for laundry, kitchen preparation, lawn care, or surface cleaning;
- mobile companion and general-purpose robots that navigate, converse, manipulate objects, and coordinate several household tasks.

Robot vacuums are already a strong smart-home category. NielsenIQ reports that 95% of robot-vacuum items sold globally were smart versions in the first half of 2024. This provides the volume and consumer-familiarity base for further domestic robotics, but it should not be used as evidence that general-purpose home robots are already mainstream.

Mordor forecasts the broader personal-service-robot market from USD 17.4 billion in 2025 to USD 41.11 billion in 2031 at a 15.42% CAGR. Domestic cleaning robots represented 56.12% of 2025 home-service-robot revenue, while elderly- and handicap-assistance robots are forecast to grow at 19.55%. [Mordor's personal-service-robot analysis](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/personal-service-robots-market) therefore describes cleaning as the volume base and care assistance as a faster-growing direction.

A separate commercial forecast for non-vacuum domestic service robots projects growth from USD 1.5 billion in 2025 to approximately USD 14.8 billion in 2034 at a 28.5% CAGR. It divides the market into laundry and folding, kitchen preparation and cooking, and companion and care. Laundry and folding represented 38.2% of 2025 revenue and is forecast to grow at 26.5%; kitchen preparation represented 33.5% and has the highest forecast CAGR at 31.2%; companion and care represented 28.3% and has a projected 29.8% CAGR. [Research Intelo's non-vacuum domestic-robot report](https://researchintelo.com/report/domestic-service-robot-non-vacuum-market) is a commercial forecast, and the figures should be treated as directional rather than independent unit data.

### Task-specific products will arrive before general household autonomy

The most credible near-term product opportunity is not a robot that can do everything. It is a robot or appliance that performs one difficult, repeated, valuable task under bounded conditions.

Laundry folding is attractive because it is repetitive and time-consuming, but clothing varies in shape, material, and condition. Kitchen preparation is attractive because it can save time and command a premium, but kitchens are cluttered and involve heat, sharp tools, liquids, and unpredictable ingredients. Companion robots are easier to deploy physically but must demonstrate sustained daily value rather than novelty.

The non-vacuum market report estimates that consumer-price robots may reliably support more than 50 household task categories by 2028, compared with approximately 12–15 in 2025. It also says fully autonomous meal cooking remains a frontier and that current kitchen systems often require partial human supervision. These claims describe an industry forecast, not a validated global capability benchmark.

The likely development sequence is:

1. A single appliance or robot performs a narrow task reliably.
2. The product learns household preferences and schedules.
3. It coordinates with existing appliances and sensors.
4. It adds conversational control and limited visual understanding.
5. It expands into adjacent tasks while retaining supervised or confirmable operation.
6. Only later does it approach general-purpose autonomy.

This path is commercially more credible because users can evaluate one clear benefit. It also limits safety and liability exposure.

### Ballie illustrates mobile, multimodal companionship

Samsung's Ballie demonstrates a different product direction: a mobile assistant that combines conversation, camera and environmental sensing, home control, reminders, and companionship. Samsung and Google Cloud said Ballie would use Gemini's multimodal capabilities and Samsung language models to process audio, voice, camera data, and environmental sensor data, adapting its behavior in real time. Planned functions included adjusting lighting, greeting people at the door, creating schedules, and setting reminders. [The Samsung and Google Cloud Ballie announcement](https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-google-cloud-expand-partnership-bring-gemini-ballie-home-ai-companion-robot) described planned availability in the United States and Korea rather than completed global distribution.

The value of a mobile form factor is that it can bring sensing, audio, and interaction to different rooms without installing a screen in each one. A mobile robot can also use spatial memory and physical presence to support routines that a stationary speaker cannot. The risks are equally clear: it may record private conversations, map the home, interact with children and pets, or behave unpredictably around obstacles.

The Verge identifies the central market uncertainty: home robots without specific use cases have historically struggled to catch on, and Ballie's indispensability and price remained unresolved. [The Verge's Ballie coverage](https://www.theverge.com/news/645853/samsung-is-finally-releasing-ballie) provides a useful counterweight to optimistic product demonstrations.

### LG CLOiD shows the shift from perception to physical action

LG's CLOiD illustrates the industrial route to domestic robotics. LG announced a CES 2026 demonstration in which the robot would retrieve milk, place a croissant in an oven, initiate laundry after occupants left, and fold and stack garments after drying. Its “Physical AI” architecture uses a Vision Language Model to convert images and video into structured understanding and a Vision Language Action model to translate visual and verbal inputs into physical action. LG says the models were trained on tens of thousands of hours of household-task data. [LG's CLOiD announcement](https://www.lg.com/global/newsroom/news/home-appliance-solution/lg-electronics-presents-lg-cloid-home-robot-to-demonstrate-zero-labor-home-at-ces-2026/) describes a planned demonstration, not commercial deployment.

LG also identifies two product categories: “Appliance Robots,” such as robot vacuums, and “Robotized Appliances,” such as refrigerators whose doors open automatically when a person approaches. This may prove more practical than putting every function into a humanoid body.
